utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, the IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All the accused are here. Presentation is like it was last Friday with the exception of Mr. Josse who is not present today. Good morning, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bourgon. I take it there are no preliminaries? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to go back immediately to where we left off on Friday when you told us about a meeting you would have had with General Krstic on the morning of the 15th of July. According to your testimony, you can -- you said that you were called by Jevdjevic to report to Krstic at the IKM at a few minutes before 9.00; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the signals officer Jevdjevic was someone else. We got this message across the radio to report to General Krstic at the IKM and Jevdjevic might well have been the person involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at that point, you were shown some documents. Now, when you were shown those documents was that before Krstic showed up or after?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krstic was there when I came, and the documents were there too. Following my conversation with Krstic, I looked at the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one of those documents was the interim combat report which was sent to the corps command by Obrenovic on the night of the 14th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was during that night. I think it was 1.00, past midnight, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it's at that time that a decision was made to send you back to Zvornik to fight the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Krstic ordered me to go back to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what I am interested in this morning, and I don't intend to spend too much time on this, is the exact contents of what was said to you by General Krstic before sending you back to Zvornik. My first question is, did he tell you how big the group, or the 28th Division, which was already in the Zvornik area ready to attack your defence line from the rear, did he tell you anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he did not have any specific information on the manpower of the 28th Division or indeed its exact location. He knew this based on a report that he received from Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, as far as you were concerned, you were sent back to Zvornik to fight this column, were you interested in finding out how big the threat was in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interested and that's why I conducted a couple of conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But General Krstic did not provide you any information regarding the strength of the column; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He conveyed the information that he had received from Obrenovic concerning the danger to the Zvornik Brigade following an incursion by the 28th Division into the brigade's area. I'm sure he didn't specify the strength of the attacking forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we saw from various documents that the mission which had been given to Dragan Obrenovic was to stop, block, disarm, capture, or destroy the column. Did General Krstic stress the importance of that mission to you before you left?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He gave me the same task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did he stress the importance of blocking the column to ensure that it would not link up with the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the fundamental thing was to prevent it from linking up with the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it you fully understood how important it was for you to prevent this because those forces might then come back and hit you on your front line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well that over-simplifies the explanation of this situation. The information that I had at the IKM in Krivace was in no way sufficient for me to take a final decision on how to use my forces, the forces that I was on my way back with, or indeed those forces that were in the defence area of the Zvornik Brigade. But I knew that the mission was clear, the 28th Division was to be blocked or crushed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my question, the last part of your answer. Now was -- did General Krstic tell you at that point on the basis of the request which was sent to him by Dragan Obrenovic, what reinforcement he was sending to Zvornik other than returning Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that it seemed that Obrenovic was in too much of a panic for no reason, and General Krstic was not convinced that the danger was really what Dragan Obrenovic would have had us believe. I can't remember specifically. Krstic told me that in addition to taking my own forces back, he would be sending in some other units by way of reinforcement. I know that some units were there already when I arrived, and I know that some other units kept arriving by way of reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that General Krstic did not believe Dragan Obrenovic when he said the situation was critical, yet he had already sent reinforcement to Zvornik; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I say he didn't believe him, he believed that the forces were there and that there was a danger. He just believed that Obrenovic was blowing this out of proportion, over-emphasising this, and that he was doing this because he was fear-stricken. Any superior must in any situation try to calm both his subordinates, any superior is under an obligation to try to show as much presence of spirit and bravery as he possibly can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was anything said at that moment concerning coordination with either the MUP or the special police?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. General Krstic did not tell me anything about any coordination. It was up to me to take a decision and see how I will be using the forces in the defence zone of the brigade and under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if General Krstic would have had at that time any information, intelligence information coming from the MUP, would you have expected him to share that information with you along with that which came from Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he had received information from the radio reconnaissance platoon, one of the units subordinate to him. He had received information from Dragan Obrenovic as well, and he had received certain information from the corps command as well. Based on what I knew at the time, he had not received any information from the MUP, at least none that he shared with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you knew what the size of the 28th Division was. Did you ask General Krstic or did he tell you whether part of the 28th Division had been stopped before reaching Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information that the 28th Division, while it was in the Srebrenica area and defending the positions that it was defending. Following its withdrawal from that area, it was no longer the same sort of military power, the same division that it used to be because now it was withdrawing in a number of different directions. General Krstic certainly knew at the time what the main axis was along which the 28th Division was attempting a break through. I don't remember him telling me anything at all about the strength, the numerical strength of the division, or indeed about what had been done up to that point to stop it and disarm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what you're telling us this morning is that General Krstic sent you back to fight a force without telling you how big the force was, how many weapons they had, and where exactly they were going; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will not go that far. He said he knew where they were going and what their intention was, at least the main body, the mainstay of the 28th Division, but nobody at all knew exactly what sort of weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at no point General Krstic would have told you that part of the column was stopped before reaching Zvornik and that prisoners were captured from that column; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in organising the return of Tactical Group 1 to Zvornik, the only thing you did before leaving in addition to speaking to General Krstic was to inquire or contact the brigade to ask about the situation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was adamant that General Krstic take the decision for me to be sent back. He was reluctant to make this move.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you called the brigade, you inquired about the situation at the 4th and the 7th Battalion, that is, because you knew, based on your knowledge of the land, that this is where the column would be heading; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on that but also based on the report from the radio reconnaissance platoon and information from Colonel Josic and the alleged intentions of a group led by Naser Oric that had performed an incursion into the Krizevici village area which was the axis and the area controlled by the 4th and 7th Battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move to the time, sir, when you arrive at the Zvornik Brigade command on the 15th of July. First, I'd like to confirm some of the things you said in your testimony, that you went directly to the office of the Chief of Staff. This was at page 30958, lines 23 and 24; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that there was, in that office already, Dragan Obrenovic, Borovcanin, Vasic, and Milos Stupar; is that correct? That was page 30959.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I think that Milo Zoric was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that the only thing that was discussed on that occasion was the situation of or created by the 28th Division, page 30959.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was only logical. That's why I was on my way back for -- what I was on my way back for, and that's the information that I was after.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And there was no mentions, according to your testimony, about prisoners of war during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just according to my testimony, no one ever said that anything like that was brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during that meeting, you testified at page 30963 that Borovcanin suggested to open the line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you can confirm that Obrenovic was of the same view; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obrenovic told me about the mission that he had received, that was quite contrary to the proposal put forward by Mr. Borovic. I don't remember Obrenovic putting forward a proposal like that. He hardly had any proposals that in any way ran counter to any of the orders received.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what about Mr. Vasic, did he tell you anything about his view that the column -- that the line should be open to let the column through?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain whether he commented or not on what Borovcanin had said, but the original proposal and the first proposal that came up about this was the one by Mr. Borovcanin. To the best of my recollection, I'd never seen him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did anyone else in meeting, and was also of the view, to the best of your recollection, that it was better to open the line and let the column through?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the others didn't really join much in this discussion. Obrenovic submitted his report to me. He pointed out everything on the map, including the tactical situation. It was based on that that I took my decision on what to do and what steps should be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did anyone in that meeting mention to you that minutes before you arrived, Obrenovic contacted the corps command to request permission to let the column go through?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. All I know is he told me about the mission that he had received from the corps in terms of stopping the advance of the 28th Division column.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was there any mention during that meeting, to the best of your recollection, that Major Obrenovic even called the Main Staff to try and obtain permission to let the column through?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if Major Obrenovic, your Chief of Staff, knowing that you were on the way back, would have done both of these phone calls, would you have expected him to let you know about what he did before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether he, in fact, made those phone calls or not. He might as well have made the phone calls and then have told me that the mission was to stop and crush the division and that, as a matter of fact, was my mission. You need to try and put yourself in my shoes at this precise point in time, and given the situation that prevailed, and you must try to remember what the focus, my interest might have been, not any previous moves made by Dragan Obrenovic. Surely, my priority was to take steps to deal with the problem that had just arisen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now that's not my question, sir. My question was: If Dragan Obrenovic did make those two phone calls, would you have expected your Chief of Staff to let you know that he did so when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he would have been expected to tell me, and perhaps he did. I simply don't have the information at my fingertips right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now who told you, sir, that there was a meeting going on in the office of the Chief of Staff? Where, how, and when did you learn about this meeting if you went directly to that office?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one told me. I knew where the office of the Chief of Staff was. I know it wasn't in my office. I went straight to his office instead. I didn't know if there was anyone in there with him and when I came in, I found those people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it's your testimony today that you just happened to fall on that meeting by coincidence?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't just stumble into that meeting, it was my intention to go to the office of the Chief of Staff, and that's what I just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you know that a meeting was going on and did you have -- did you intend to participate in that meeting when you arrived at the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My intention was, first of all, to meet the Chief of Staff. I had no idea who else he was with at the time. Even if I'd known that there was a meeting in progress there, I would certainly not have waited for the meeting to be concluded and try not to disrupt it. I would have walked straight into that room just as I did anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you had no idea that Borovcanin was there and waiting to put his forces at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I had no idea about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned a few moments ago that Obrenovic gave you the -- his report and that he used the map to do so. Did he indicate to you the number of positions of the units on the line? Maybe I can make my question more precise: Did he tell you exactly how many soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade were present in each of the battalions?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He knew it and I knew it too, there was no need for him to tell me where each of the battalions were and what their respective strengths were. The order was to assume positions and the order applied 100 per cent across the board. I knew what the strengths were and how many men were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So there was no mention by Obrenovic to give you an updated report as to exactly how many soldiers were in the trenches on the line for each of the battalions, you took that for granted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody could give you that sort of information with any great degree of accuracy, not the battalion commander let alone a brigade commander. What he did tell me, however, is that none of the battalion positions had shifted, that the front line had not been penetrated, that the 6th, the 4th and the 7th Battalions had managed to fend off all of the attacks coming from the front line. He also pointed out to me the positions of the additional forces that he had brought in by way of reinforcement in Snagovo, Crni Vrh, and Planinci. He also shared with me what he knew about the present deployment of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Looking at the exact situation for Snagovo and Crni Vrh, did Dragan Obrenovic tell you that he had to remove a platoon from each of the battalions, if not a company, in order to form some kind of a intervention platoon to send to Snagovo and Crni Vrh thus depriving each of the battalions of important resources?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did the right thing. He regrouped the brigade forces where this was indispensable and he also engaged additional forces from the battalions which were under no threat from the -- either from the front line or from the rear. He told me that he had established two companies as temporary forces under the command of Mr. Maric and Mr. Jovanovic, and he told me where the companies were deployed. He also told me that a unit of the Ministry of the Interior had arrived from Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what about the forces from Bratunac, did you decide where the forces coming in from Bratunac would go or had he already made his decisions concerning these forces?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he told me that the forces that had arrived from Bratunac had been sent to the area of command of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that in addition to telling you about those two companies that he created, that he told you about the reinforcements that he had called in or -- I'm looking for the exact answer -- and that he deployed. Tell me to the best of your recollection what were those forces that he told you about during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me how he had carried out a manoeuvre with some of the elements from the brigade. In addition to the ones that I had just mentioned, he also spoke about the engagement of the elements of the tank company that remained in Zvornik. There two self-propelled guns, 57 millimetre, and one APC and one Praga. All that was in the general area of Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is units coming from the outside. What other information did you have from Obrenovic concerning units which were not from the Zvornik Brigade that were coming in?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned a MUP unit from Doboj and a unit from the Bratunac Brigade as well as the fact that Mr. Borovcanin was there and that his units under his command were ready to be engaged pursuant to my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: One question I forgot to ask you about concerning General Krstic. Did he tell you before you left on the 15th in the morning that you would be in command of all forces in the area to face the threat posed by the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all knew what kind of threat they could pose. I don't remember that he said anything special about that threat. Based on the reports that we were privy to at the time, we were all able to conclude that this indeed was a threat that had to be taken seriously and that we had to take the right position vis-a-vis that threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe my question was not precise enough. Did he tell you that you would be in command of all forces in the area to face the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not have to tell me anything to that effect, nor did he indeed tell me because it was self-understood. In my area of responsibility, what was attached to me and what was under my command, if I was the most senior officer, then I was in command. That's how things were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I take it on the basis of this answer that later on on the 17th, on the 16th and the 17th of July, when additional forces from the outside came in to participate in a combing operation, they were also under your command, that goes without saying; is that true?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when these forces used the Orahovac school to sleep and use as accommodation, was then the Orahovac school used by the Zvornik Brigade command or by something else?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where the company that had arrived from the 16th Krajina Brigade spent that night in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you saying that you are not aware that forces coming in to participate in the search of the terrain used the Orahovac school as accommodation starting on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the company did arrive in the territory of Orahovac and that on the 16th, the task -- Obrenovic were getting in touch with that unit and issuing the task to the commander and show him the terrain. They started searching the terrain but they soon stopped that and they spent the night in the territory of Orahovac. It was summer. I don't know whether they spent the night in a facility or under the sky. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, are you saying that this is information that was important to Major Obrenovic but it was not important to you to know where these forces were staying and were billeting?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What mattered for him at the moment was where to find them, where to meet them. He did not really have to know where they were billeted. And I'm sure that he met up with them somewhere on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, when you drove past the Orahovac school and you saw the earth that had been moved, as you testified, did you see that the Orahovac school was being used by those forces?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I passed by the burial site on the 17th in the evening, and that is a bit before the school. I took an asphalt road by the school. I did not notice anybody. It was on the 17th in the evening and all the units were engaged on the scouring of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I come back to that meeting. Did you ask Major -- did you discuss any other topics about reinforcement with Major Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the 15th meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, the meeting on the 15th when you arrived at the brigade and you speak with Obrenovic. We talked about Doboj and Bratunac reinforcements. I'm talking -- did you talk about any other deployment of units of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that there were any other units there or that any other units would arrive in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I take it that you never asked Major Obrenovic where the military police company had been deployed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What military police company are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I think there might be something -- either it's my mistake or a mistake in translation. I'm talking about the military police company of the Zvornik Brigade, and I'm asking you whether you asked Major Obrenovic because you said you did not discuss any other deployments, where was your military police company? Where was it deployed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that it had already been deployed in the area of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And he didn't tell you that he would have given part of the military police company to Drago Nikolic as you testified?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, on the 15th, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, you'll agree with me that as a brigade commander such as yourself, the military police company is about the only flexible resource you have to deploy on the battle-field. That's what you call, in military language, your reserve; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually it was no reserve at all and its main task was not to be engaged in combat. However, truth be told, it was often used for that although this was not its planned use and very often that company or, rather, parts thereof was often engaged on all sorts of tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And whenever the military police company was used for combat tasks, they weren't deployed by Drago Nikolic, were they?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to combat and when you engage a military police company, it was not Drago Nikolic who decided on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, as we say, sir, the man on the ground is always better placed to evaluate the tactical situation, would you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on who does the tactical evaluation, whether it is an officer or a foot soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I suggest to you that if one person knew the real strength of the 28th Division getting ready for a clash with the Zvornik Brigade, that was Dragan Obrenovic; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He knew approximately what the strength of the 28th Division was, but he didn't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So he had been there two days organising companies, pulling soldiers from the lines, sending interim combat reports to the corps, but you knew better than him what the situation was with the 28th Division; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Bourgon. I didn't know how much I knew at that moment about the 28th Division in the territory of Zvornik. However, in any case, the 28th Division was not lined up so there was no way for us to count heads. It was walking through the forest, through the mountains in several parts, and certain elements of the Zvornik Brigade did come in contact with the 28th Division. The first information spoke about 200 to 300 men. The next was about 1.500 and then 3.000 men. We had all sorts of information. And I knew that I would learn the truth when I arrived at the IKM and when I compared the information that I received at the command from Dragan Obrenovic would -- my personal insight on the ground and the information that I received from the battalion commanders who were there on the spot. I believe that only then would I be able to complete the information which again did not mean that it would be completely accurate and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, I suggest to you that if there was another person who was very much aware of the tactical situation involving the 28th Division, that was Vasic who had also been on the ground for the past two, three days fighting this column or taking measures against that column; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where Mr. Vasic was in the course of the previous two or three days and what he did. I assume that he did not go to the area where Dragan Obrenovic was, so I don't know what information Mr. Vasic was privy to at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that during that meeting, Vasic never told you where he was for the past three days and what he had seen about the column. He didn't share that with you at all.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vasic did not brief me at all. He was there, he was present. Whatever troops he had at his disposal was a PJP company subordinated to Mr. Borovcanin and on the strength of his forces, so Mr. Vasic could not offer me nor indeed he did offer me any other forces. His forces were deployed around Kula Grad and on the brims of the city of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But during that meeting, did you ask him, And you, Vasic, what do you know? What can you do for me today? Did you ask him any questions?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked the people who were there what they had, what forces they had. I told you what they had. Mr. Borovcanin was in command of the combined MUP forces composed of the special brigade from Sekovici and the PJP from the public security centre in Zvornik. As for any other MUP forces that were in the general area, they were under the command of the MUP staff which was either in Bijeljina or in Zvornik, I'm not exactly sure where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that during that meeting, it was suggested to you to let the 28th Division through simply because the people who were there in that meeting knew very well that the Zvornik Brigade, even reinforced with Tactical Group 1 and the outside group sent as reinforcement could not stop the 28th Division. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you think that if it had been possible to destroy the 28th Division and the column, that Obrenovic would have done so before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To destroy does not mean to kill everybody to the last man. You destroy a unit when it is not capable for any further combat. Obrenovic did take measures which he did, he set up ambushes and ambushes are a special type of combat by way of which less powerful forces can inflict damage on more powerful forces grouped in a convoy. The data that we had on the 15th in Dragan Obrenovic's office is something that Dragan Obrenovic knew best. Vasic did not know as much. Borovcanin probably knew even less because he had only arrived there. And I, as the commander who had received my orders to block and destroy the 28th Division, without going to the field and establishing what the situation was, for me to make such a decision in the office, it would have been simply terrible and it would have immediately been reported that I had not taken my task seriously. If I had done that, this would have been construed as me refusing to carry out an order or not having carried out my order completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, sir, I fully agree with you that during that meeting, you could not relinquish your mission such as fast as this and you had to see for yourself. I understand that. But my proposition is is that once you were on the ground and once you saw what Vasic, Obrenovic, and the others had seen for the past three, four days, you understood that the Zvornik Brigade with could not stop the column and you agreed with them and that's why you let the column through; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The column had already stopped. It was in a solitary state in the territory of Planinci. On the 16th in the morning, they actually tried to block the barrels with their own bodies which is a desperate measure, a measure taken by a person in dire straits, in a desperate situation. We had -- have some intercepts showing people from the 28th Division were not able to do anything, that's what they are heard saying. We have statements by their commanders about the situation in that division. We have information related to Dragan Obrenovic on the 16th in the morning at the command post of the 4th Battalion by an officer of the 28th Division. All that showed that the 28th Division was as good as destroyed at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, one last question on this issue. If the column had been stopped as you say by Major Obrenovic, the mission was thus successful and the column was not going anywhere and would not reach the 2nd Corps. Why didn't you simply, if you were so strong, capture the column and that would be the end of it without any fighting? Why didn't you do that if you were so strong?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th, I entered negotiations with Mr. Semso Muminovic. The column of the 28th Division at that time was even further from us from our front part, the 2nd Corps had not managed to achieve any successes. There was no combat going on. The situation was calm at that moment, and I was thinking about the tasks that had been given to me and how I would be able to accomplish it very elegantly by entering into negotiations and letting the column go through, especially those who were not armed. On that day, I asked for those who were carrying arms to surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We'll come back to this issue, page 17 line 3, it's been brought to my attention that there was something -- a mistake concerning 3.000 men which does not appear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Page 17 line 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The only full sentence I have: "The next was about 1.500 and then ..." what seems to be "... 2.000 men." Is this --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's where it should read 3.000 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 3.000 men, okay. Thank you. Do you agree to that, Mr. Pandurevic? This is the part when you said -- "The information spoke about 200 or 300 men. The next was about 1.500 and then 3.000 men." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that previously, Your Honour. However, in my last answer, I never mentioned any numbers at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This was a little -- a couple of minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I leave it in your hands, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I would just like to ask you a few questions about the time before you left for the IKM on that day. And did Obrenovic give you any information concerning who was at the forward command post and who was on duty there before you left?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date are you referring to? You are saying when I left from the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Leaving the Zvornik Brigade command to go to the forward command post as you testified, before leaving, did Obrenovic tell you whether -- who was on duty at the IKM and who was there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he said anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: He did not tell you that any special security measures had been taken for you to lead the battle from the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the IKM had been under threat, I'm sure he would have told me that. Since that was not the case, there was no need for him to say anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And he did not tell you about any special duty system that he would have organised for you to lead the battle from the IKM?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, that IKM had been there for a long time. It did not all happen on the 15th. And we were not thinking along the lines that you are asking me. What this implied, there were always signalmen at the IKM, in crisis situations there was somebody on duty, an officer always present there. This is what all that implies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, we know that. What I'm asking you is that was there anything special done? It's not every day that the commander of the brigade goes to the forward command post to lead the battle from that area. I'm saying was there anything special, other than the normal situation put in place by Dragan Obrenovic before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty was -- the duty service was organised at the IKM even before I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I needed as an answer. Now, did you discuss before leaving the Zvornik Brigade command on the 15th at around -- in the early afternoon as you testified, did you discuss any other topics with anybody else while you were at the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you knew from your telephone conversations in the morning that Dragan Jokic was at the brigade command. Was it not important for you to know where the engineer resources were at the time, and did you not try to speak to him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that Jokic was the operations duty officer and the engineering resources have nothing to do with it. If there had been someone from the logistics, I should have asked him about the logistics -- the rear units then. The Chief of Staff is my closest associate, the Chief of Staff is the person who can give me the best and most accurate information regarding anything which is exactly what he did when I arrived at the command on the 15th. I no longer needed any information from anyone else. I don't even remember seeing Jokic on the 15th. I don't remember that he was sitting in the office of the operations duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you anticipate, sir, at that time before leaving the command having to use engineering resources to fight the column?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Where did you ever see that; engineering resources being used to fight a column like that? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, if I just look back at the testimony of General Kosovac, he explained that in order to block a column you might very well use engineering resources. As far as I'm concerned, it's a very well-known fact. But I'm just asking you, did you anticipate the need to use engineering resources to fight the column? I mean, you can just say "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this had been mechanised or an armoured column, a column using roads along which one can place obstacles and perhaps even minefields, well, then engineering resources might have been used. However, given the kind of terrain that the 28th Division was crossing, you could only use foot soldiers, no machines whatsoever. And anyway, how could one possibly have used a machine there. Perhaps to help construct and reinforce positions at the front end, but at this point we had that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you'll agree with me that when you were for the past three years the Zvornik Brigade had been facing an enemy to its front and had dug in positions to face an enemy coming from the north. Would you agree with me that now that you have suddenly an enemy coming to your rear, that you need to change your complete defence disposition, and that you need engineer resources to prepare the line to face a threat coming from the rear. Do you agree with that; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree, Mr. Bourgon. I would need to explain to you the many things belonging to the field of tactics and how in a tactical sense, units of resources should be used in a situation like this. I'm not quite sure that we have sufficient time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, I spoke recently to the military expert who testified here on behalf of the team of Drago Nikolic, and he explained to me exactly that -- the change, when you have an enemy coming to your rear and you have to change your complete defence positions or disposition of your trenches, and it goes way beyond changing the weapons from facing to the north from facing to the south and that it includes a lot of digging and a lot of reorganisation which takes a lot of time and a lot of resources. Just tell me whether you agree or disagree with him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Sorry, is he putting a conversation he's had with somebody?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm simply putting the foundation to my question. I don't know what this objection is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, are you putting evidence in the case or are you putting a conversation you've had with somebody else outside of court?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm putting to the foundation to my question so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's a simple enough question, could you answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you are also making a statement, and the question that Mr. Haynes is raising is whether you are offering that statement as part of -- as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not offering evidence, Mr. President. I'm simply putting a foundation to a question, and then the witness understand can answer whether he agrees with that or not. It's not evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I plan on asking many similar questions based on knowledge that I may have gained from various sources. And as long as he's not trying to make it evidence, I think he can ask questions like this all day long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is precisely what Mr. Haynes raised. I mean, if he is suggesting that this is how it is and this is part of the evidence, then obviously there are problems, but using it as a foundation for his question is another matter. So let's proceed. Your question was very long, Mr. Bourgon. I think I better read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My question, Mr. President, if I can try to make things as quick as possible is simply: Reorganising the defence line to face an enemy coming from the rear requires lots of resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you need us to repeat the question to you, Mr. Pandurevic, or are you in a position to proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not necessary, Your Honours. I'm able to answer the question. I think Mr. Bourgon is here discussing something that is a well-known fact in the field of tactics. An attack from the rear, forces being introduced based on a plan to unsettle a defence and to make it easier for other forces from the front line to carry out an attack. Or there could be an airborne attack with a landing at a certain facility, again in order to distract the defending forces and stretch them out. In situations such as these one must always plan for some reserve forces to engage these new attacking forces. There might be situations where you'd need to use the engineering resources to block an area where a landing is expected. Nevertheless, the situation at hand is entirely different from everything that I've been talking about so far. We had the 28th Division, forces of the 28th Division, being hounded from the Srebrenica area and driven towards the Tuzla area. They had not been infiltrated in order to crush the Zvornik Brigade. They were at this point moving along, trying to use stealth, if possible, to reach the area of the 2nd Corps as quickly as possible. They were not successful in this, rather, they were detected, their presence was detected, and they were blocked. The 2nd Corps was then the principal force that tried to give them a hand. They tried to open a new front line in order to link up with them by carrying out an attack from the front line. The Zvornik Brigade did not at all shift any of its defence lines that were contiguous with the 2nd Corps, the lines were merely reinforced. Some of the forces being used for that purpose by Dragan Obrenovic, some of the forces that had arrived from elsewhere, and Tactical Group 1 were entirely new forces. They were unrelated to the forces engaging the 2nd Corps, but they were engaging the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'll leave it at that. At the headquarters on that morning, you knew that Mijatovic was at the command. Did you try to speak to him before leaving the command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know he was there. I asked whether he was around and whether I could speak to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you spoke to him, we have -- the intercept was shown to you, that was one of your conversations, and he provided you with some detailed information with respect to the ground. Didn't you want to have an updated information from him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on all these conversations, you've probably realised that I never exchanged a single word with Jokic about the tactical situation or the deployment and disposition of forces or indeed the fighting in progress. I knew that I could not obtain the adequate information for it, and there were all sorts of reasons that I'm not going to go into -- going into right now. I remember it, however, that Mr. Mijatovic some time before was the commander of the Baljkovica Battalion, and I realised that he was a person who was exceptionally familiar with the area. I asked him to provide me with a precise disposition of our forces as well as reliable information on the alleged incursion of groups led by Naser Oric to Krizevici village area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's exactly my point. When you arrived at the Zvornik Brigade command, you attend this meeting with Obrenovic. Coming out of this meeting and before leaving to the IKM, didn't you want to speak to Mijatovic that he could provide you that type of information because he knew very well the terrain.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been pointless, this would have been hearsay. Any information he had, he had been given by Obrenovic. I wanted to go straight to the source, Dragan Obrenovic himself. Why on earth would I humiliate him by speaking to someone else when he was the source?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it would be humiliation to verify information you obtained by Obrenovic by speaking to Mijatovic; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information conveyed to me by Mijatovic via the radio is information that he had obtained from Dragan Obrenovic. It wasn't his own information. So how could I possibly verify this information with him and how could I learn anything about whether Obrenovic's information had been accurate to begin with or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how do you know that it was not his own information when he gave that to you over the phone a few hours earlier?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he said he'd spoken to the boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you know that Sreten Milosevic was at the Zvornik Brigade command that morning because he was also involved in that conversation you had before leaving the Zepa area. I take it then that you did not speak to Sreten Milosevic before leaving the command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Weren't you interested to know, sir, before engaging in a battle with the 28th Division whether the brigade had enough bullets?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew they had what was necessary. There was always a combat kit at the battalion station attached to the battalion command. I knew that each of the soldiers had a full combat kit on them, and the third combat kit was kept at the brigade's rear station. You see that later on during the fighting I asked for reinforcements in terms of ammunition and certain kinds of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you know as well as I do that the ammunition within a brigade goes up to 72 hours maximum, and you had no information what kind of ammunition was used in the past 72 hours. But nonetheless, you're saying that you knew that the brigade had sufficient ammunition and that you did not need to speak to Milosevic in that regard; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The norms you are talking about, the 72 hour norm, it's not something that I'm familiar with. It's not part of the JNA doctrine. I'm not sure where you got your information, it's probably other sources you're drawing on in other armies. In the VRS, we determined this in relation to each individual mission, how many combat kits would be used. Given the conditions in this situation, and we were defending, we had sufficient ammunition, especially the small arms ammunition. We were never short of that. If that had been a problem, that probably would have been the first thing for Obrenovic to bring up when speaking to me, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you interested, sir, in finding out whether the brigade was able to provide food to the units coming from the outside which were sent in as reinforcement? Was that something you would have liked to discuss with Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't like there was a single loaf of bread and this was meant to be not to feed the whole command. The food supplies that were there were sufficient for at least a whole week.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what about the transport resources to move the soldiers around on the battle-field as well as to transport the food. Is that something that you would have liked to discuss with Milosevic that morning?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I'd gone to that kind of detail, I would have stayed there for God knows how long. These are things that go without saying, and they just happen as they are meant to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you knew that the duty officer was at the Zvornik Brigade command, and I take it that you did not speak to the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered that question, haven't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get a time, a date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm talking all the time about the 15th before leaving the command. Mr. President, I would like to get five more minutes to finish this topic and just to go until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we have an agreement with Mr. Pandurevic that we stop after an hour and 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then we can stop here, Mr. President. I will just say to clarify, to answer my colleague, that I was always talking about before leaving the command on the 15th, but we'll get back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, getting back where we left off before the break, and I'm referring to the 15th of July, when you are still at the command of the Zvornik Brigade. And just to summarize your position, when you arrive at the brigade, you had a meeting with Dragan Obrenovic during which you discussed the situation created by the presence of the 28th Division, you did not deem necessary to speak to Jokic, the chief of engineers, and who was the duty officer that morning. You did not speak or try to speak to Mijatovic, because his information was secondhand. You did not speak to Milosevic, assistant commander for logistics, because he had no question -- there was no questions of logistics as these things just happen, as you say, and I take it that you did not speak either to the new duty officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, all of it. All I did was all the things that I've testified to already in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the expert witness who testified in this case, Lieutenant-Colonel Landry, on 25 September at page 26261, he said that if one person knows the ongoing situation, it is him -- I'm sorry, that was General Kosovac, he said, If one person knows the ongoing situation, it is him. My question is the following and I'd like to read a part of what General Kosovac said: "When any officer is leaving and the most senior officer who will stand in for him is there, he is duty-bound to create such conditions in which the officer who will stand in for him has all the information about the situation in the unit that will enable him to reach an appropriate decision in view of the commander's wishes and goals, otherwise the officer standing in will not be able to make an appropriate decision in an emergency." Sir, on this basis, I'd like to know if, before leaving the command on that day, you told the brigade duty operations officer that you were leaving and where you were going?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Are we still talking about the 15th of July or some other day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely. I've been talking all about before leaving the command it was quite clear and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood it to be. Let's proceed. Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I left the command, and when I took over the command of the tactical group and was off to the general Srebrenica area, it was Dragan Obrenovic who stood in for me as brigade commander. The previous answer that you quote might imply an entirely different situation. Someone stands in for someone else for an hour or two or a day, perhaps, and then this other person conveys to him information that might be relevant. But I was in no position to inform Obrenovic on what might or might not be happening over the following 20 days. On the other hand, establishment-wise, he was my deputy and he knew about as much as I did. He had all the information that I had. All the information that was available to me was available to him when we were together at the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, this is not my question and maybe my question was not clear enough. What I'm saying is, did you feel it was necessary before leaving the brigade command on the 15th of July to tell the duty officer that you were leaving and where you would be?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In that case, I should have called a new duty officer on the 16th to tell him as well where I was. I left and there was another person who was discharging my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, under normal circumstances, we have seen from the duty officers' notebook that when you went to see your lady friend in Celopek, you would tell the duty officer before you left where you were and leave a phone number. I'd like to know why, in this case, before leaving the brigade command to wage the war from the forward command post, you did not feel appropriate to warn the duty officer before leaving?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't noticed that the date you were talking about was the 15th of July, the day when I left the command, and that's why I provided the answer that I did. As you put it yourself, I am by nature a responsible man. Whenever I was with the brigade and whenever I was in effective command of the brigade, I would always leave information pertaining to my whereabouts, and I was at all times available to the duty operations officer. I was always in a position to receive information and, if necessary, react. On this particular day, when I arrived on the 15th, everyone knew exactly what was going on and where I was off to. Everyone was perfectly clear about that. I did not specifically speak to a duty operations officer on the 15th to tell him that I was off to the IKM; although, I had seen the first entry in the log book dated 11.45 and the handwriting was that of Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, it is your testimony that before you arrive at the Zvornik Brigade command on the 15th of July, everyone knew even before you arrived that you would only attend one meeting and then go immediately to the forward command post to lead the battle. What you're saying is that everybody knew this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them knew exactly when I would arrive or whether I would be attending a meeting. I didn't know this myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you take it for granted that a duty officer, the brigade duty operations officer knew that you were going to the IKM without you telling him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He should have known. And he should have been able to infer where I would be off to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And now being the commander of the Zvornik Brigade and having been away -- having been away for almost ten days, you did not feel appropriate if only to open the door and take a peek in the duty operations officer's room and to ask if everything was okay. That was not necessary for you to do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I hadn't tracked down the Chief of Staff, I probably would have done just that. If I hadn't previously met Dragan Obrenovic, if I hadn't received information from him, the next thing for me to do would have been to go to speak to the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it that you did not check if there was somebody in the operations room or department?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That door was normally open. I did throw to glance to see whether somebody was there. However, during the conversation with IKM at Krivace, I knew that Dragan Jokic was on duty that morning. I don't know whether he started the duty that day or the day before. I didn't know that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you ask Dragan Obrenovic where the operations people were?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations people work in the operations section of the staff, one of them was with me at Zepa. I didn't ask, I didn't inquire about the others because those were his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it was not important to you -- for you to know where the other people in the operations department were?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what, Mr. Bourgon, the commander does not have to poke his nose in everything, to put it that way. He has to know exactly who he should talk to and who he should seek information from. It is not his job to inspect various officers to see who is there and who isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, when you left or before leaving the Zvornik Brigade command on that day, did you see the military police leave going to Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I have noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well according to the testimony of some of the military police, I'll just refer to one, and that was at the transcript at page 6542, the question was: "And where were you physically when you received that order to go to Rocevic? Where were you on duty at that time? "A. I was in the standard barracks. "Q. Approximately, can you tell me approximately what time of day was this? "A. It wasn't in the early morning. It was again in the afternoon hours." Did you see the military police at the Standard barracks that day and did you see them leaving for Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see from that answer that one of them left in the morning and the other one left in the afternoon. This does not give us any precise time as to whether it was at noon or at 1400 hours. I don't know if I saw any police officers, I did see soldiers in the barracks; however, if I'm on my way, I don't stop. I don't ask every foot soldier where they are headed in order to find out whether somebody is headed for Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But the fact, sir, that Dragan Obrenovic was in the command that morning, and that military police were sent to Rocevic on the same morning, is that information you would have expected him to give you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you confirm that other than the information you obtained from Dragan Obrenovic before leaving, you had no other information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the expert witness who testified in the defence case of Drago Nikolic said that a commander should always ask for a full briefing when he returns to his brigade. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did the same and I received full briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, on 11 February, at page 31238, line 25 to page 31239, line 19, you describe what you did when resuming your functions as brigade commander on 26 September 1995. Do you remember testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You said, and I quote: "Since I met Obrenovic for a brief period and he was preparing to leave for the Krajina, I shortly told him about some of my experience from the combat operations and my stay in that area, and then I took up the regular duties of a commander, which means I talked to the officers from the staff, the operatives first and foremost, in order to be informed with the situation in the brigade." You also said: "And looking at this work book for that day, as it says, the battalion commanders and artillery battalion commanders had reporting sessions." Sir, on this basis, you'll agree with me that upon your return to the Zvornik Brigade command on 15 July, you did not get the full briefing as you should have done, according to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that question has been interpreted correctly, but we are talking about two entirely different situations here. On the 15th of July, I came with a very clear task and objective, and that was to deal with the newly arisen combat situation operation. The first person who briefed me about everything was my deputy. He was the one who could do it adequately and professionally. And both of us remained in the area of responsibility of the brigade and both of us were in the centre of combat activities. On the 26th, he was the one in command of the new brigade and he left, and this was all done on the move. There was nobody else available to me to provide me with information save for the person who was acting on behalf of the Chief of Staff, and that was Milos Maksimovic. And later on, in order to be provided with the complete information about the situation in the brigade, we held the battalion command briefing. You wouldn't expect me to call all the battalion commanders on the 15th when I arrived and hold such a briefing while combat was still ongoing in the area of Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So can we agree that due to time constraints and the emergency of the situation, you were satisfied that you could not or you were not able to get the full briefing that you required.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What day are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Always the same day, always before leaving the brigade command on the 15th of July. I'm asking you whether it is because of time constraints and the emergency of the situation that you did not obtain a full briefing before leaving?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been a stupid thing to -- for me to do as a commander. I could have wasted time on briefing by the first battalion commander about the situation in Lokanj, knowing full well that nothing was going on there. I was briefed by my deputy. He pointed to the problems in the brigade and I dealt with the problem. I had my regular briefing session on the 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, during his testimony, General Kosovac, who testified as an expert in this case explained, and I quote: "Now in exactly this scenario which you described a little earlier, and that is because of time constraints the commander is not able to get the full briefing, would you expect him to arrange a meeting with his Chief of Staff at the earliest opportunity in order to get that briefing?" The answer of the general was as follows: "Yes, that's absolutely so. He would initially be asked to be informed of the most important facts, and then he would say, You will give me more detailed information at such and such a time or after such and such a thing takes place. So he would tell him when he expected the full briefing." Do you agree with this statement from General Kosovac?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any difference between what I'm trying to explain and what Mr. Kosovac said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what event he is referring to here. However, looking at the sequence of events that he points out, this is exactly how things developed on the 15th, and my meeting with the Chief of Staff. On the 15th at that meeting, Dragan Obrenovic informed me about the burning issues, and then we went together to deal with the task ahead of us. On the 16th in the evening, I again met with him and he provided me with the fresh information in detail; on the 18th, it went even further; and on the 23rd, we had this briefing of the battalion commanders. And this is exactly the sequence of events as Mr. Kosovac portrayed it in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's very useful for my next section. What I would like to do at this time is return to the alleged conversation you had with Dragan Obrenovic on 16 July. This time I'm not interested in what Obrenovic told you on this occasion, but rather I want to look at what you did or did not do after the conversation. Now, you can confirm, of course, that Obrenovic told you that there were people shot dead and buried in Orahovac in that conversation; you recall saying this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could understand the introduction into your question, you said you were not interested in that at all, but I can confirm that he did say that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I want to clarify that you did not know how many people had been shot in Orahovac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I want to clarify that the people shot dead in Orahovac, you knew that this referred to the prisoners coming from Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was told, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did not know whether there were still prisoners held in Orahovac school when you had that conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me what had happened in Orahovac. He never told me that there were more people being held at the Orahovac school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's exactly my point. You don't know if there are still prisoners while you're speaking with Obrenovic in Orahovac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you knew of course that many members of the 4th Battalion lived in the vicinity of Orahovac school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some did. Whether there were many of them or not, I don't know, but some did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I can settle with "some did." According to your testimony, you knew from Grujic that prisoners were held also in Petkovci school and Pilica school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that I remembered him having mentioned the two schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And according to your testimony, Obrenovic also told you about a conversation he had with Ostoja Stanisic and the fact that prisoners held in Petkovci were executed both in the school and near the dam; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you did not know if there were still prisoners held in the Petkovci school?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Obrenovic did tell you that members of the 6th Battalion were involved in collecting dead men around the school and driving them to the dam; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ostoja Stanisic told him that at the villagers' request, some people had indeed taken part in the removal of the bodies that had been scattered around the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you knew that many members of the 6th Battalion lived in the vicinity of the Petkovci school?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that many men from one company resided in the same village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can we settle for some members of the 6th Battalion lived in the vicinity of the Petkovci school?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you had no information about the situation at the Pilica school, that's exactly when you are having the conversation with Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did not know if there were still prisoners who were held there and who were still alive?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You did not call the corps command to clarify the situation and obtain more information about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In your testimony at page 31385 lines 16 to 19, your answer was the following: "He had received information from Drago Nikolic in the form and content as he, and when I say 'he,' I mean Dragan Obrenovic claims. Then, the least he could have done was to call the corps command and clarify the issue with them and undertake steps for such things not to occur." My question is the following: What happened with your own saying? Didn't you feel important it was to call the corps command and do exactly what you said Obrenovic should have done?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please first read the question and then my answer? That's for our future reference. At that moment I wanted to get the complete information to know what had been happening in order to be able to send a complete report to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it was not appropriate, the situation was not urgent enough for to you call the command immediately even though you were told that people had been shot and buried in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, in view of all the information that I was privy to at the time, I believed that I had to check certain things first before I sent any reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So calling the corps command could wait until you obtained more information and that's why you gave the night off to Obrenovic, so he can report with that information in the morning, there was no urgency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you consider sending Obrenovic to the corps command or keeping Obrenovic at the forward command post and going yourself to the corps, or maybe that was not important enough to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, since the command of the Zvornik Brigade and the brigade had not received any orders from the corps command to receive prisoners of war and take care of them in any way, the brigade command could not, without any additional information, report back to the corps command. The fact that Drago Nikolic said something to Drago Obrenovic, and that was that he had to stay and receive the convoy of vehicles transporting prisoners of war, did not mean for a single second that it was his task to kill these people. The prisoners of war save for being in the territory of the municipality of Zvornik had nothing to do with the Zvornik Brigade, and I can understand Dragan Obrenovic's understanding who said in his interview conducted on the 3rd, 4th and 5th of June, 1995, that they were his concern and that the Zvornik Brigade was in charge of executions.
