And this -- he said only upon the intervention of Mr. McCloskey. His initial answer was the Zvornik Brigade was not tasked with that, and then he changed his answer to "yes." I will never understand why he changed his opinion and why he decided to take that responsibility upon himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you had information that prisoners were shot and buried in Orahovac, you had information that prisoners were executed in Petkovci school and at the dam, you had information that soldiers from the 6th Battalion were involved in moving the bodies around, but yet you basically said it's none of my concern, the brigade is not responsible, and my report to the corps can wait in the morning; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this is correct, but you failed to mention one more thing. I knew that this was organised and carried out by the security organs from the Main Staff level, and later on I learned that the Zvornik Brigade security organs were involved. That was my initial information and the reason why my first report was drafted the way it was and sent the way it was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not talking about the information you learned later, I'm talking about the information you gained just minutes ago from Dragan Obrenovic, and at that time he did not provide you information that the security was responsible for this, and I don't need to recall what exactly you said about Obrenovic, we made that very clear. Did you not call the Main Staff at least to confirm what the information was about the prisoners and what was the intentions of the Main Staff regarding the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, your question involves different points in time. The events did not follow the sequence as you presented. Obrenovic informed me about the fact that the security organs of the Main Staff were there and that they had brought a column in and that was on the 16th. He also told me what they asked from Jokic to do and what they asked from municipality officials to do, so I knew it at the time. It is not as if I learnt it only here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But, sir, that's not my question. You did get information on the 15th about the presence of prisoners. On the 16th of July, you are informed that prisoners were shot dead and buried in Orahovac and executed in Petkovci. You know that soldiers from your brigade are involved in moving bodies around, and you did not call the Main Staff or you did not send a combat report immediately to say what is going on there; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it was not important for you to warn them of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was important, it was. It was absolutely important, however, it was also dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You had a secure line with the brigade duty officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you could dictate to him immediately on the phone a report which could be sent to the corps command by secure means; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but luckily enough for -- or misfortunately, those were duty officers who knew much better than me what was going on and they were in constant communication with the duty officer of the Drina Corps and other people at the Drina Corps, also with the Main Staff, and the people who were involved in all that, who had done it; so they were in a position to inform anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you had no information about what the brigade duty officer knew at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic, it was -- he was on the 15th and Trbic on the 16th, and I didn't know at the time the extent of their knowledge about the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did not call the brigade duty officer even though you sent Obrenovic just to do that, to speak to the brigade duty officer according to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I sent Obrenovic -- I didn't want to call just anybody. I thought that that would be the best way and manner for us to obtain complete information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you agree with me it would have been much quicker than sending Obrenovic simply to call the brigade duty officer and ask him if he knew anything about that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been faster, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, according to your testimony, at no time that night you yourself inquired with the brigade duty officer about the prisoners in other schools or executions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent Obrenovic to check all that and collect information. That's why I did not call anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My question is not why, we'll get to that later. Is it your testimony that that night, you did not inquire with the brigade operations duty officer about the presence of prisoners in other schools or executions?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, my previous answer spelt that for you. I did not call anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that there were a number of conversations between you at the forward command post and the brigade operations duty officer that evening; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the exchange of information between the IKM and the operations duty officer, that did take place. However, I was at the observation post, and the information was conveyed from the weekend cottage where the IKM was. I don't recall any direct communication with the duty operations officers. I did not remember hearing his voice. You could see that it says in the log book of the duty operations officer that the information was conveyed to the commander at the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So let's take a look at e-court P377, please. I'd like to have in English page 151 and in B/C/S also page 151. I think we have the original that we can give you, sir, and I ask you to look at the entry at 5769 -- on page 1769 [sic], where it says "message from Zlatar." Page 5769, it says: "Message from Zlatar that a parcel sent off from Badem half an hour ago, it was reported at 2015, reported at IKM." Are you saying that this information was not communicated to you that night by the duty officer at the IKM?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, what I'm saying is exactly the other way around. I received this information, but not directly by talking to the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The duty operations officer, which one?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we are looking at this and we see that the man involved was Trbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you did speak to Trbic that night at 2015?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you I don't remember. I most probably never spoke myself to the operations duty officer directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But was this information communicated to you then by somebody?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. There was a signals officer manning the switchboard receiving messages and relaying them to me, and then I would instruct him what to convey to others. I wasn't a signals officer myself, I was a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Was there an officer on duty beyond -- beside you at the IKM that night?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not when I was there. I remember the chief of signals, Milisav Petrovic, I remember that the intelligence officer Mica Petkovic was there for a while. The security, the soldiers, the signalsman, there was always someone around.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, since you've been so helpful since the beginning of your testimony in telling us what the entries in the operation duty officers' notebook means, what was the parcel which set out from Badem that night?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably a number of soldiers from the Bratunac Brigade. Based on my recollection, they arrived that evening and they joined the 16th Krajina Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have in e-court please page 5770, the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I refer you sir to the second entry where it says: "30 soldiers from Bratunac at 2100 hours, IKM informed regarding their engagement." Now, that information was communicated to the IKM, did you receive this information?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did just as all the other information that was relayed to the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, here it says that 30 soldiers from Bratunac, so that means that the parcel of the previous entry must be something else. Do you remember what the parcel was from Badem?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says first that the parcel was off and now it says the parcel has arrived, the 30 men or whatever. So it's one and the same thing, one and the same men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I look at the next entry down where it says: "At 2108 hours, the IKM was informed that Milenko Marjanovic from the military police has been captured, and they want to see if there is any possibility for an exchange." Did you discuss this information with the brigade duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The IKM was informed, that's what it says. I was at the IKM. Someone probably told me. I can't remember specifically right now, and I can't tell you what you're asking me to tell you, Yes, I was told this about specifically at such and such a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But my question is: Were you told this information on the line -- on the secure line between the forward command post and the brigade command by Trbic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a secure communication line that was used to relay this, and I can't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you speak at 2108 hours to Milorad Trbic who was the brigade duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I gave you a general answer to these questions, didn't I, about the contacts between me and the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not asking for a general information. I'm asking if that entry at 2108 was a discussion between you and Milorad Trbic who was at the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm telling you that I did not speak directly to the duty operations officer. Maybe this was, in fact, occasionally the case, but what he recorded, the IKM was informed. If it was me personally that he was speaking to, he probably would have written something to the tune of, I relayed this information to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I draw your attention to the last entry on this page, where it says: "At 2155, the commander requested 100 dry daily rations, rifle grenades, and hand grenades to be sent to Orahovac, and he also wanted to know how much ammunition has arrived today." The commander, that is you, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you speak to the brigade duty operations officer on that occasion at that time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two possible alternatives: The first one that you had been adamant about, that I spoke to him personally; and the other option would have been the signalsman got in touch and said, The commander seeks this or seeks that, because if you have an operations duty officer, he can't just make an entry like this: I am seeking this or I am seeking that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's move to page 5771. And there are two more communications between the IKM and the brigade command that night. The first entry at the top of the page: "Message from the IKM that the unit from Bratunac is sleeping at the barracks and the Praga is to stay where it is." Do you recall discussing this information with Milorad Trbic who was the brigade duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember discussing these issues at all to begin with. At the time, it struck me as not so important. What is recorded here that word got through from the IKM, meaning someone had conveyed my order for the men from Bratunac to sleep in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I draw your attention to the second last entry at the bottom of this page where it says: "The security centre reported at 2317 hours that enemy groups have been spotted moving from Kusonja to Crni Vrh and that this was passed on to the commander at the brigade IKM." Now, the commander, that is you; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you still deny that you spoke to Milorad Trbic that night?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not denying it. I told you a while ago about the two alternatives, what the possible alternatives would have been. If he had got in touch with me directly and told me directly, that was one thing, but he might have relayed this through a signalsman. One thing is certain, I do not remember talking to Mr. Trbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, looking at this page in the book again -- one minute. If we can go back to page 5771. This is an entry at 2210 hours from the 1st Battalion asking from one loader, one excavator, and a dump truck with a tarpaulin to be in Pilica at 0800 hours. And this information was conveyed to Jokic and to Milosevic. Sir, if you had spoken to the brigade duty operations officer that night instead of sending Obrenovic, you could have obtained that information, and you would have known what was going on in Pilica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have obtained that information but it states clearly who the requests were conveyed to. I testified in chief that on the 18th at Baljkovica, Jokic told me that he had received this request for this machine to be sent over to Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But that night, this request was addressed to the brigade command from the 1st Battalion. How come Obrenovic the next morning on the 17th was not informed of that if he spoke to Trbic that night?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was informed about what Trbic had told him. The conversation may have taken place before this entry and maybe after this entry. Either way, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you knew that many members of the 1st Battalion -- let's correct that, you knew that some members of the 1st Battalion lived in the vicinity of the Pilica school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did not call the 1st Battalion if only to get a report about the situation; whether there was still prisoners in the school, who was guarding them, and what was happening to them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I had never given an order to that battalion in that respect. I didn't and Obrenovic didn't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you had information from the 15th that there were prisoners in Pilica, and you have information coming from Obrenovic that there's been executions in two places. Don't you want to call to see what's happening with the prisoners in Pilica? Are you not interested by this information?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about the prisoners in Pilica, the school building on the 15th. I had not heard about any executions anywhere until the evening of the 16th and that was the reason I dispatched Obrenovic to Zvornik to gather information for my sake on all the other events in all the other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly my point. While Obrenovic is gone to the Zvornik Brigade command, and you've already conceded the fact that it would have been quicker to call yourself, while Obrenovic is away, you did not call the 1st Battalion to find out what was happening with the prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't call. His command was in the village of Manojlovici, the distance being about 10 kilometres from Pilica. I don't think the commander would have relayed anything at all frankly, even if he'd known anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, being the good commander that you were in 1995, weren't you interested in calling the 1st Battalion if only to let them know that the presence of prisoners in Pilica was taken care of by units which were not from Zvornik and this had nothing to do with the brigade, at least so that you would reassure them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't call them and I didn't tell them about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And knowing that executions had taken place in both Orahovac and Petkovci, did you consider sending an order to the 1st Battalion at least to say: Do not get involved in any way with the prisoners who are held in Pilica? Did you consider doing that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even know that they were involved to begin with or that anyone had ordered them to get involved. Therefore, I simply had no reason to call in order to tell them not to get involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I'm just talking, sir, about the information that you did have, not on information you learned later, but on the basis of the information that you did have, didn't you feel and did you consider calling them to ensure that your brigade would not be involved in the killing of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I have harboured a suspicion to begin with that my brigade was involved in anything like that. Those prisoners were brought there under escort by other people. The first information was that there would be a triage and that they would later be exchanged. Why would I anticipate that some killings might take place?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because you obtained information that some were shot dead in Orahovac and Petkovci, and you at least want to warn your battalion not to be involved; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have reasoned like that. I could have been thinking that those people had been killed, the people who, as it later turned out, had been killed over there, but I could also infer that perhaps those people were still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly my point, sir. If they were still alive, maybe you could have saved them, but I'll move on to the 6th Battalion command. Can you confirm that you did have secure means of communication from the forward command post to the 6th Battalion command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the first thing you said previously, that those prisoners were still alive and then I warned the 1st Battalion, and had I warned the 1st Battalion maybe they would have still been alive. You know who carried out the execution. You now who had brought those people there. It depended in no way on the 1st Battalion or indeed the command of the Zvornik Brigade. As to the second part of your question, we were in contact with the 6th Battalion. Was there a wire link, a safe one from the IKM, or did this go through a switchboard is not something that I can be certain about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: According to your testimony, even though you learned from Dragan Obrenovic that the 6th Battalion was involved in some way in moving around the bodies and that there were executions in the school and at the dam, you did not call Ostoja Stanisic if only to get a report about the situation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had spoken to Dragan Obrenovic and conveyed to him that type of information. Ostoja just happened to know about this and the villagers had asked for the dead bodies to be removed, so that's what they did. Was that a crime? Does moving the dead bodies constitute a crime? Well, then that is up for debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My point is that on the basis of this information, didn't you want to find out or ensure that the 6th Battalion was not involved deeper into these executions?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean involved deeper? The man said it was all over. How can he go any further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll make my question more clear. You had information that coming from Dragan Obrenovic who got this information from the commander of the 6th Battalion that personnel from your brigade were involved in moving bodies who had been executed in the school. My question is: Were you not interested in ensuring that the implication of members of your brigade did not go beyond moving around bodies?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the man was speaking in past tense, it was something that was over. He said the bodies had been removed. I don't see what else the 6th Battalion might have done there or what else the 6th Battalion might have been involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if it's in the past, it doesn't matter, I don't need to speak to the battalion commander to find out if my brigade is involved; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was another thing that was on my mind, namely that I shouldn't launch into conversations with certain people and thus broaden the circle of people from whom I would be requiring information because this would have reached the ears of the probable perpetrators in no time at all. If there was a truth that I could have gotten at before this Tribunal does, this would have had all sorts of ramifications for some people. If you think that an organ like this can investigate the actions of a commander, a security investigator, then you're not right because the security people do not have the authorisation to do that. You have the instructions for the work of the security organs and the instructions say that they must investigate any crimes within the jurisdiction of a military Tribunal. They must make sure that no evidence is removed, they must search flats, they must seize goods and possessions. They must issue summons, they must interrogate, they must detain, and so on and so forth. So what are you expecting me to do in a situation like that? To sound the alarm at full blast and launch an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm referring to is the exact moment after Dragan Obrenovic left to the Zvornik Brigade command upon your instructions, and what I'm saying is that there is no broadening of information. The information came from the commander of the 6th Battalion, and you will agree with me that you could have ordered Ostoja Stanisic to report to the IKM to explain to you what had happened there if only, because you did not know as you said, whether prisoners were still alive there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have reported to me or to the Chief of Staff. He reported to the Chief of Staff which was tantamount to reporting to me because I received the same information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's my point. You don't know if there are still prisoners being held there and alive, and you did not call Ostoja Stanisic; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the third time, Mr. Bourgon, I'm telling you it was over, past tense, far back in the past, Ostoja says. This is over, no one is alive, the bodies that were lying around the school building have been removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I'll just remind you your answer at page 41, lines 20 to 22 -- or 21 to 23: "Q. But you did not know if there were still prisoners held in the Petkovci school?" Your answer was: "I did not know." Not knowing whether there are still prisoners alive in the school, we're not talking about the past tense, could you call Ostoja Stanisic to come to the IKM and explain to you what was going on?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there may have been a misunderstanding. I didn't know if there was anyone still alive in the school building before Ostoja spoke to Dragan Obrenovic, but after his conversation with Dragan Obrenovic, I knew that there were none left, no one was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Pardon me, sir, but that's the first time you say this, and when I questioned you as to the exact content of your conversation with Dragan Obrenovic, never did you say that everyone had been killed there. So are you changing your testimony now?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not changing my testimony. I'm saying they were killed. All or not, it's just a word that I might use, but if I say they were killed, the meaning is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll move on, sir. You know that our position in this case is that on the 13th of July, Obrenovic did not receive any information from Drago Nikolic about the prisoners. Nonetheless, based on what you say, Obrenovic told you on the 16th of July -- I take it that you did not attempt to reach Drago Nikolic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Drago Nikolic in those days. Obrenovic left on the evening of the 16th and I expected that I would track him down, but he tracked down Trbic, not Drago Nikolic. I did not speak to Drago Nikolic about this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my question was: You did not speak to him, but you did not consider or try to reach him by calling the brigade operations officer, for example?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you I didn't speak to him. I didn't see him, I didn't seek him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that if Drago Nikolic was, as Obrenovic said, the first person who received the information or the order concerning the arrival of prisoners, then he would have been the right person to speak to to clarify the situation. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. If Obrenovic found him there on the 16th then he would have conveyed that to him and maybe he would receive the more accurate information than the information that was conveyed to Obrenovic by Trbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, you will agree with me that you could, through Trbic or other means, order Drago Nikolic to come immediately to the forward command post to provide you with a report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean on the 16th in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, on the 16th in the evening, sir.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, again, of course we -- our position is that the conversation between Drago Nikolic and Obrenovic on the 13th July never took place, but according to your testimony, Drago Nikolic could have informed you as to how many prisoners were taken in the Zvornik area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he did not convey that to Obrenovic. If Obrenovic did not talk to him, then Drago Nikolic waited for the column of his own will and did things on his own, and he took the five or six policemen without Obrenovic having approved that move.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well that's not my question and I'm not sure I understand your answer, but the question is very simple. If you had ordered Drago Nikolic to come to the IKM that night, he could have told you, based on your testimony and that of Dragan Obrenovic, he could have told you how many prisoners arrived in the area; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree he could have and he should have. If he knew, he did not have to wait for my order or request.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And of course you know our position in respect of that - and I don't have to say it again - but he could also have told you, if you and Dragan Obrenovic are correct, where the prisoners were taken that night or that day on the 14th of July, sorry?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it is your position that he did not speak to anybody, that he wasn't there, then he could not have told me. If your position, however, is different, and if the position is that he was there and that he talked to people then he could have told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We're not talking about my position. We're talking about your position and the information that you had. According to your testimony, you got information from Obrenovic. On the basis of the information that you say you were in possession at the time, if you ordered Drago Nikolic to come to the IKM on the 16th, he could have told you what the MPs he allegedly used, including Jasikovac, did in respect of the prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he could have come, he could have said that, he could have told us where he had met up the column, how many people were with him, where the column had been taken, with which senior officers he had met, who had carried out the executions, where were all the people at all times. He could have told us all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, based on the information you obtained from Obrenovic, I don't think he could have told you where the executions took place, because Obrenovic never said anything of that to you, but he could have told you what the -- any military police he allegedly was given that night, what they did when the prisoners arrived, whenever they arrived. That's what he could have told you; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least that. At least the things that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And why did you not consider -- why did you not call Drago Nikolic or ask for him to come to the IKM?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not call him because I had sent out Obrenovic to collect information, and I placed more trust in what Obrenovic would come back with than whatever Drago Nikolic would have had to convey.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that information could wait in the morning after Obrenovic had slept at his place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he did not have much sleep. He left late. He arrived early. And the information was already there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, I take it that after your conversation with Obrenovic on 16 July, you did not attempt to reach your commander of the military police company, Jasikovac, if only to get a report from him as to what he did with Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I did not call him. The information that I had was such as to the whole operation having been conducted from the highest level, that there was a suspicion that some individuals in the Zvornik Brigade might have been involved, at least according to Obrenovic's information and what he told me. I could not have conducted a selective investigation in order to establish what an X, Y, Z policeman had done without establishing at the same time what Nikolic, Trbic, and others did, and under whose orders they had done what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did not issue any order to ensure that members of your military police company would not be involved in the guarding or any other manner with the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you could have contacted the brigade duty operations officer and ordered Jasikovac to report to you immediately?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just as with the previous person that you spoke about. However, according to the information that I had on the 16th in the evening, things had already taken place at those locations, and I fully believe that those policemen in question were no longer engaged anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, wasn't it important for you to confirm that the members of your military police company in your brigade were not involved in any crime? Didn't you want to confirm that after hearing of the executions in Orahovac and Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, no member of the Zvornik Brigade had participated in the executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, after your conversation with Obrenovic on 16 July, I take it that you did not call nor attempt to call Dragan Jokic, your chief of engineers, if only to get a report on the use of the engineering resources which were used and ensuring that members of the engineering company were not involved in the burying or in any other matter with the prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th in the morning, I met with Jokic and I asked him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But I'm referring to the 16th after your conversation with Obrenovic, you did not attempt to call Jokic to find out what engineering resources had been used and by whom?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that Dragan Obrenovic on the 14th in the evening, he told him how the equipment had been requisitioned and who requisitioned it. It was not Jokic who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you had no idea, sir, who had buried the bodies who were executed at the Petkovci school or at the dam; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To this very day, I don't know who participated in the burial of the bodies at the dam. At that time, according to Jokic, those were the two machines from Birac Holding and Jasenica quarry and BGH700 from the engineer's company. The machinery was run by a soldier from the engineer's company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I have more questions concerning what you did and could have done that night but I will stop here. However, just I'd like you to confirm whether any of what I'm going to say you disagree with. Following your conversation with Dragan Obrenovic on the 16th of July at the forward command post, according to your testimony, you sent Dragan Obrenovic to the Zvornik Brigade command to find out more information and you gave him a night off. You did not call the brigade duty officer to find out more information even though you had a secure line of communication with him. You did not call the corps command to try and obtain more information. You did not call the Main Staff or attempt to call the Main Staff to obtain or provide information. You did not send an immediate report even though you had secure means to do so. You did not call the 1st Battalion. You did not call the 6th Battalion. You did not issue any orders to prevent no one from Zvornik Brigade to be involved with the prisoners. You did not try to reach Drago Nikolic. You did not try to reach Dragan Jokic in respect of engineering resources and you did not try to reach Jasikovac in respect to the military police resources. Do you disagree with any of these statements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And to be clear, you are limiting this to the 16th of July only.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The night of 16th of July immediately after, following the conversation with Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Bourgon, let me put it this way: This question sums up all of your previous questions and now you're asking me to sum up all of my answers and make one simple answer out of it. Generally speaking, I agree with what you put to me. Nevertheless, had I been there as an attorney-at-law on the evening of the 16th, in my capacity as an attorney-at-law not a commander, had I had the time to reflect peacefully on what I could possibly do, maybe not all of these things would have come to me but some certainly would, the best part, I would say. Nevertheless, we have to imagine the situation as it was, the reality on the ground and what was going on. There is something else that I didn't do. I didn't ask permission from the corps or the Main Staff to do what I did on the 16th. That's another thing that I didn't do. I didn't call any of these people that you mentioned to check these things with them because I believed that the information available to me by way of Dragan Obrenovic was sufficient. I also had to consider all the potential consequences of any action that I took in terms of opening up the corridor and in terms of negotiating with the opposite side. As for calling any of the security officers and discussing this subject with them, I don't think it would have made any sense because I wasn't likely to obtain any information at all from them, not even to the extent that I received from Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, as you testified at some point in the evening of 16 July, the passage of the column was interrupted pursuant to the agreement you and Muminovic agreed to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, in these circumstances, I suggest to you that there was plenty of time, that you had the necessary communication means, and that it was both feasible and possible for you to take the actions we just discussed and which you confirm you did not do. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was feasible and possible to take different kinds of actions including the ones that you mention, but the passage of the column of the 28th Division was disrupted and that was not a mitigating circumstance because the danger was all the greater for fresh forces of the 2nd Corps being infiltrated through that corridor behind the lines of the Zvornik Brigade defence. What would have become of me then if something like that had happened? I did this in full awareness and I took action myself, and that was my foremost concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, on this basis, my question is the following: What did you do at the IKM the night of 16 July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was awake until well past midnight. I was at the IKM and I was maintaining contact especially with those forces that were in the open corridor because there had been a physical contact that had been established between the BH Army soldiers and the Republika Srpska Army soldiers. I think by 3.00 or 4.00 that morning I was again awake and again up and ready to monitor the developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I now move on to the 17th of July in the morning, that's immediately the next morning. According to your testimony, when Obrenovic returned, he informed you of the following, and this can be found at page 31084, line 9, to page 31085, at line 7, and this was on the 9th of February. You said that Milorad Trbic, the duty operations officer conveyed -- sorry, I did not say you said -- you were told by Dragan Obrenovic that Milorad Trbic who was the duty operations officer conveyed to him the following: That Drago Nikolic was not there because his brother had been killed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, maybe I was looking over this weekend because you said "brother." Now, it's not his brother who were killed, but I think for you it's something that you use even though it was his cousin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we say cousin or relative, depending on the exact kind of kinship involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I just looked into that over the weekend. But you know that it wasn't Drago Nikolic's brother who had died. Did you know that at the time or were you told that it was his brother?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it was his brother or not, but I've learned since during the trial that this person who was killed was in fact not his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Trbic also told Obrenovic that he confirmed that the prisoners accommodated in the schools in Pilica and Rocevic were executed there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Trbic would have confirmed to Obrenovic the killings in Orahovac and Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Trbic also mentioned to Obrenovic, according to your testimony, that some machinery from the engineer company had been used to bury the bodies of those who had been executed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, having learned that information from Dragan Obrenovic on the morning of 17 July, I understand from your testimony that you did not take any action with respect to what you learned from Obrenovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No specific action, but I spoke to Dragan Obrenovic on what would be the best thing for me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, even if I agree with you that the fighting the column -- well, at that time was no longer fighting, but at least it was leading the operations of the column going through your lines was a very important part of your obligations on 17 July, I suggest to you that there was sufficient time, that you had the necessary communication means, and that it was possible to take all of the actions that we discussed together and that you confirm that you did not take in the night of 16 to 17 July; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the latter part of your answer about the night between the 16th and the 17th, yes, that's right, but then you said that I had sufficient time and sufficient means of communication on the 17th; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's what I'm suggesting to you.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm telling you that I spoke to Dragan Obrenovic on the morning of the 17th. We considered the information. We knew what the 16th had been like and what the requests had been by the corps and the Main Staff about my decision to open up the corridor. Later, I learned that an interim combat report had been requested. I waited for that date to pass, for the corridor to close, and then on the 18th I wrote up an interim combat report. It had a number of addresses, and all the addressees found it sufficiently explicit. They knew exactly what it was about and what I meant when I wrote that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not talking about what you did concerning the column and the 28th Division. I'm calling -- -I'm talking about actions concerning what you obtained from Dragan Obrenovic about the executions. Now, I quote from page 31085 to 31086, the question was put to you: "What action did you decide to take about the information Obrenovic had given you about the prisoners?" And your answer was: "I told him that we would resume that conversation later as soon as our job was over, and our job at hand was to let the column of the 28th Division go through." Do you recall saying this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting to you, I come back to my previous question, is that while you were letting the column of the 28th Division go through, I suggest to you that you had the communication means, the time, and the possibility to take all of the actions we discussed that you did not take on the night from the 16th to the 17th, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Those are actions that I could have taken but that is with hindsight and post facto. But that would have done nothing to diminish the crimes that happened. I thought what I should do at the time is think of a way to address the corps command and inform them about all these issues, and what I can't help but wonder is why no one else left a trace of any sort of note at all on what had gone on, with me as the only exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, sir, the -- I'd like you to confirm that even at this point in time after your conversation with Dragan Obrenovic on the morning of the 17th, despite all the terrible things he announced to you, you still did not know whether there were still some prisoners who were alive and who could be saved; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the information I received was that people were there and were shot there. No one said anything about anyone else being brought over, any persons remaining or any persons to be shot at a later date. My information did not suggest anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. Because you did not get this information did you ask Dragan Obrenovic: Do you know if there are still prisoners we can save? Did you ask that question?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well I'm telling you, the information said there were no persons left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, once again, sir, I think that this is contrary to what you said before but I will move on. Some other people might be interested in exploring this answer. I simply suggest to you that on the morning of the 17th of July, having received such information from Dragan Obrenovic, it was even more important for you to take such action than it was on the night of 16 July. Do you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I received information as to where those people were detained and that all of them were shot. This rules out everything else. This entirely rules out the possibility of someone being left behind. There was no information suggesting that. I never had any reason to believe that there was anyone left there who was still alive. The information that I received was dire enough. When you're told something like this, what can you possibly do? You know it's nothing to do with you, and how do you cope? You can't just dart out through the door and take action that very minute. You have to stop, pause, and a take some time to think and consider your options.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And for you, sir, the taking the time to stop, pause, and think was to wait until the 18th of July when you sent that additional interim combat report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, part of the information you obtained is that engineering equipment from your brigade was used to bury the prisoners. Now that's precise information that your brigade is involved. Don't you think it was more important to take action on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that the machine did belong to the engineering company of the Zvornik Brigade and the driver was a member too, but the machine itself was not in the possession of the Zvornik Brigade and it certainly wasn't my private property. It was just something that the VRS was using, and I wasn't the one who sent that man on that mission. Therefore, it was not my place to investigate any steps that he took in an isolated context and outside the context of an overall investigation or, indeed, investigating any action taken by any other persons involved in that specific event.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, during your examination-in-chief an intercept was shown to you, that is P1206, at -- involving a conversation between yourself, General Krstic, and Trbic on 17 July at 0615 hours. Do you recall seeing this during your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this conversation at 6.15 happened after your conversation with Dragan Obrenovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you had an opportunity to mention this to the corps commander, and you did not mention anything to him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke about that in chief and I explained why and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed what you said, sir, is that you did not do because General Krstic did not mention anything in relation to your interim combat report of 15 July. Do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So because the general didn't mention it, then you said, It's not appropriate, I don't have to tell him.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, yes, I didn't raise the issue. I knew that I'd be dispatching an interim combat report, and I knew that I would personally get in touch with him and raise the issue, broach the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But not before the 18th of July at the earliest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the 18th that the interim combat report was dispatched.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did have as of 15 July -- 17 July in the morning, much more information than when you submitted your interim combat report of 15 July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was receiving information and sending interim combat reports. It was in lockstep, and you could see that the amount of information was increasing as I was sending out further combat reports. I certainly was not concealing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, again I remind you what you said about your own saying, that the least Obrenovic could have done when informed about the killing of prisoners is to call the corps command and clarify the issue with them and undertake steps for such things not to occur. That was at page 31385. Are you saying that this did not apply to you on 17 July even though you had the corps commander on the line?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, on the evening of the 14th, Obrenovic had information to the effect that people were being shot in Orahovac or that they had been shot. Therefore, he was not able to prevent this either. Maybe his reasons were similar for not informing anyone given the information that he had received from Drago Nikolic. I did inform the corps command, however, both in writing and orally. I spoke to the corps commander. What you seem to be insisting on, something that I could have done on the 17th or the 18th, that being to call Drago Nikolic and order him to investigate the crimes which we had found out in the meantime had occurred in the Zvornik area. Well now, you can go to Drago Nikolic and you can ask him yourself what he would have done in a situation like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that the reason you did not say anything to General Krstic on that morning is because in fact all this information about the executions you learned from Obrenovic not on 16 July but much earlier on 15 July; isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. But my mode of reporting would not have changed even if that had been the case. However, I only found out on the evening of the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, that morning - I'm talking about the 17th of July - according to your testimony is the same morning that the three colonels showed up from the Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three colonels from the Main Staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during your testimony, you described, that was at page 31092, lines 7 to 16, when and to what extent you spoke to the three colonels and that you basically responded to their questions without providing any additional information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I take it then that you did not mention anything to the three colonels concerning executions and all the information you obtained from Dragan Obrenovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I said that military logic would imply for me to say something about that. I may have been guarded by the idea that my reports mentioning these prisoners had already been dispatched. No one from the superior command reacted to this and that included them. Another reason would have been they were from another superior command. They were not my direct superiors. And the only person I wanted to raise these issues with at the time was General Krstic and no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, sir, you would agree with me that here you have a chance to speak directly to the representatives of General Mladic and to let them know what has been happening in the area of the Zvornik Brigade, and it is your testimony under oath today that you did not bring the subject at all with them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, and under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that the reason you did not say anything to the three colonels that morning is because in fact, all this information about the execution you learned from Obrenovic on 15 July at the IKM; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can move into closed Mr. President -- private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, so concerning that we never had any warning about the content of your testimony before this Trial Chamber that you would be talking about a conversation between you and Obrenovic on the 16th of July, is that something you kept as the commander's surprise for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be a surprise for many, the way I testify may be surprising because they maybe thought that I would select information. Before I even received the indictment, I had decided to testify before this Tribunal. That was never out of the question. I had decided long before that that I would testify before this Tribunal and that I would say everything I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that when you and I met at the United Nations Detention Unit in December of 2005, you never mentioned having any conversations with Dragan Obrenovic on the 16th of July; do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not enjoy the privileged position with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you met with Eileen Gilleece, you never said or told her that you had this conversation with Dragan Obrenovic on the 16th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had received information from him on the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, according to the report that we have looked at in this courtroom, and I've asked that question before so I did not think it was necessary to come back, but it says here that: "I was informed by the Chief of Staff on the 15th of July," isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained the mistakes that appear in this report. This is one of them. At one point, a reference is made to the chief of security who informed me about things, but that was another mistake. The information came from Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But I'm not talking now about the mistake, I'm talking -- you met with Eileen Gilleece, an investigator from the Office of the Prosecution, with the aim of helping and solving this case. Did you tell her on that occasion that you had a conversation with Dragan Obrenovic on 16 July 1995 about the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed but you need to redact. Go ahead, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll look into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, sir, then let's go back to the events of the 15th after you left the command of the Zvornik Brigade. You testified today that other than for the meeting with Obrenovic, Vasic, Borovcanin, and others, you did not discuss any other topic than the 28th Division; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The only topic was the 28th Division and the tactical combat situation. Those are the things that we discussed at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, in these circumstances, and in accordance with the testimony of General Kosovac and Lieutenant-Colonel Landry and your own behaviour in September 1995 that we recalled, I suggest to you that being a very good commander, as was established on Friday, the 13th of February, you did order Obrenovic to meet you at the IKM that same day on the 15th of July so that he could provide you with all the information you needed to resume your functions as commander and to lead the battle against the 28th Division. Isn't that the truth, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, at the command he conveyed all the information to me, the information that he had, and then we left together. I went to the IKM and he went to the command of the 4th Battalion, which was one and the same place. And then we got additional information on the spot. So there was no need for him to meet with me again because any unnecessary movement around the battle-field poses a risk. Second of all, there was nothing else discussed at the meeting save for the topics that I am telling you about. I may have been a good commander, I'm not saying that I wasn't. I probably was. But I was not a clairvoyant. I was not a prophet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, you will agree with me that by the 14th of July -- sorry by the 15th of July, by the time you had this meeting at the brigade command, that Obrenovic was fully aware of what had gone on in Orahovac the day before; do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to him, on -- according to what he told me on the 16th in the evening, yes, that was probably the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And knowing this information, it is, I suggest to you, that he would have told you if you did not ask for him to meet that day, he would have told you: I need to see you that day to discuss something. Would you have expected something like that from Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not tell me any such thing, and as for expectations, expectations may vary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, who was at the IKM when you arrived there on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that several times, I told you who I remember. I believe that at the same time with me or a few minutes later, the chief of communications arrived, Petkovic, Petrovic was there, some signalsmen were there, and there were some couriers as well. As for the rest, I don't remember any others. Later on in the afternoon, Ljubo Bojanovic also turned up at some point. And before him, Mr. Brano Grujic was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, did anyone else arrive at the forward command post before Branko Grujic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you whom I found when you arrived up there. They had already been there. I had been at the observation post some 300 metres away, whether somebody arrived in the meantime, whether somebody spent some time there or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, according to the testimony of Dragutinovic in this case, that was on page 12599, 12600, on that day you issued an order to Galic to deliver some information and to brief Dragutinovic with respect to the tactical situation. When and where did you see Galic that day?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Galic was asked to convey my order to Mia as to where to send the tank company. At that time, I believe Galic was in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you -- it was inside the barracks that you met Galic, because you told us that you didn't speak to anybody else but Obrenovic, so it was at the barracks that you issued that order?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to look at the log book. This was said at the IKM, and it was recorded that Galic was told to convey the message to Milutinovic [as interpreted]. I don't remember any meetings with Galic. This information could have been received by the duty operations officer Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, as you testified, when you arrive at the IKM, the situation was not critical and not -- certainly not as critical as it was put to you in the meeting with Vasic, Obrenovic, Borovcanin and others. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was almost calm. The only difference was in the area of the 7th Battalion on the left flank from where one could hear sporadic fire being opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, page 83, line 15, the name "Milutinovic" appears and it should read "Dragutinovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Line 15, wasn't it? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, so you will agree based on your last answer that there was no threat to the municipality of Zvornik, and it was clear that the column intended to break the line at the intersection of the 4th and 6th Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a day before the column had already passed by the town of Zvornik and no longer posed a threat to the town of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the likely point of impact if the column was to force its way through the line was where, according to your reading of the situation at that time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been in -- more in the middle of the 4th Battalion rather than at the intersection between the 4th and the 6th Battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, when you arrive at the IKM, you did have secure lines of communication with the brigade command as well as with the battalions.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was the case with the 7th Battalion, whether I had a direct wire line with them or if I had to go through the 4th Battalion. In any case, I did have radio communication with the 4th --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: With the 7th, the interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So just to clarify, you did have wire communication with all battalions and the 7th, maybe you had to go through the 4th, and in addition to that you had radio communications. That's the way I understand your answer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understood my answer correctly. There was a direct wire line with all the battalions. I believe that the communication was done with the 7th and that I had to go through the companies of the 4th Battalion in order to get to the 7th. And we also had direct radio communication via RUP-12.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I take it that you did contact your battalions to inquire about the situation on the line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information from Obrenovic that the situation was quiet everywhere but in Baljkovica. That's why I focused on that area and I had contacts with the commanders of the 4th, 7th, and 6th Battalions. We were in constant communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, that's one thing, for example, I wanted to confirm, because Lazar Ristic said before this Trial Chamber on 17 April that you did call him. So you confirm speaking with Lazar Ristic on the afternoon of 15 July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, you testified that Branko Grujic told you, and I quote: "He simply arrived and asked me how come there were prisoners in some schools on the territory of Zvornik municipality. I think he mentioned the school in Petkovci and the one in Pilica." So I have referred to that quote before, but my question is the following: In the circumstances at the time where you were sent back to the Zvornik area to defend the forward defence line of the brigade against the threat posed by the 28th Division coming from the rear, you will agree with me that the transfer of a large number of prisoners of war placed in schools which are located close to the potential combat area and within villages where members of the brigade and their families live, that this was a factor which you had to consider. Do you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I include the words "additional burden" in my interim report. This was not my task or obligation. The way I was thinking was just along the lines of what you have explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So one reason, for example, why you had to consider the issue of the prisoners is that the prisoners could escape and thus could add to the considerable threat represented by the 28th Division. Is that one of the reasons?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say that my thoughts went along those lines. Mr. Grujic told me that there was a degree of dissatisfaction and misgivings on the part of the people in the area where the prisoners were accommodated, and there was a likelihood that some of the soldiers who hailed from the area may have thought that their homes were under threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that was important for you as a brigade commander because you don't want the soldiers to desert the trenches to go and protect their families; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's very important. As soon as Ljubo Bojanovic turned up, I had a word with him and I asked him about his information on the prisoners of war in the territory of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, in your testimony, you mention that the persons who were there when Grujic showed up could not provide you with any information concerning the prisoners. Who were these persons?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably Captain Petrovic who had returned from Zepa with me and some signalsmen or soldiers, but I never thought of asking them anything because what could a foot soldier have told me about such a matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Bojanovic was not there at the IKM when Grujic told you about the prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he appeared a bit later. I believe that he had taken a shift of soldiers somewhere and then came to the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, not being able to obtain information from anybody, that is before Bojanovic arrived, you are telling us today that you did not call anyone to obtain more information before he arrived; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that the first person you would call to find out if indeed prisoners had been transferred in the area of Zvornik would be Dragan Obrenovic who was acting as commander in your absence and who would know what happened in your absence. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I had received information which did not point to anything extraordinary, both with regard to the lot of the people and their -- the length of their stay, Bojanovic appeared very quickly, I talked to him, and what he told me put my mind at ease in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well I don't know, I'll move on to what Bojanovic told you when he arrived just to see -- so you can explain to us how much your mind was at ease when he arrived. But what he told you, according to your testimony, is the following. He said he had information about a column driving by -- prisoners driving in front of the brigade command, but he could not provide you with any other information. Can you explain to us how that information put your mind at ease?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it sufficed for him to tell me that no order had arrived from the command with regard to the prisoners, that he had seen buses driving in the direction of Bijeljina. He told me that it was likely that some of them had kept for a while but that they all be dispatched to Bijeljina. Second of all, when Krstic sent me from Bijeljina from Zepa, he never mentioned any prisoners who would be transported or were already to be found in the territory of Zvornik. I'm coming back to the real time, the real situation, and the way I was thinking at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, sir, just let me for one last question for today maybe, this was on page 30984, and the question was: "What did Ljubo Bojanovic tell you?" And your answer was: "Ljubo Bojanovic told me that he knew that some buses with prisoners had passed by the command and that they had gone in the direction of Bijeljina, but whether they stopped in some schools in the Zvornik area or not, he did not know so he said. And he said he did not know that the command of the Zvornik Brigade had received any task concerning the prisoners of war." Now, what I'm putting to you, sir, is that on the one hand you have Grujic who tells you that you have prisoners present in schools in your area, he gives you two specific names including Pilica and Petkovci. On the other hand, you have Bojanovic who tells you that all he knows is that he saw buses passing by the command but nothing else. Sir, in these circumstances, I suggest to you that you could not have your mind at ease and that you needed to find out more in order to accomplish your mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mind was put at ease with regard to that. I may have been unsettled about something else. My task had nothing to do with the prisoners. I was given a task at Krivace and I got down to it. What you have quoted just now is exactly the same what I'm saying now. The late Bojanovic even claimed that he didn't know anything about the prisoners and that he learned about them only ten days subsequently. It would be similar to me saying that I only learned about the fall of Srebrenica when I saw myself leaving the town on TV. That's the kind of statements people provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, you did not think at that time, this is your testimony, you did not think of picking up the phone, the secure line with the brigade operations duty officer to ask him: Did you see any prisoners arriving in our area? Did you do that, sir? Did you consider doing that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. I've told you over and over again. You see, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we can stop here for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow, as you know, we are sitting in the afternoon at 2.15. We are adjourned.
